The History of Cells and Cell Theory

MYP 4 Science · MYP 4 / Grade 9 Biology · Criterion A · 75 minutes · Prepared by Mr George Apidi
Guiding question: Why did it take until the 1600s to discover that every living thing is made of cells?
🎯 Start here

In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork and saw rows of tiny boxes. He called them "cells". Why did it take about 170 more years before anyone said every living thing is made of them?

Notes

For most of human history nobody knew that living things were made of cells: not because people were not clever, but because nobody could SEE one. Cells were discovered only when the technology arrived to look.

Notes

Before that, many people believed in spontaneous generation: that living things could appear from non-living matter, such as maggots from meat or mice from grain. It took two centuries of microscopes and experiments to replace that idea.

STEP 2 · EXPLORE

The history of cells

15 min · Activity 2

🎬 Videos for this lesson

▶ The wacky history of cell theory (TED-Ed)Watch once through, then again with your pen ready: you need the names, the dates and what each person actually saw.

How the theory was built

  • 1590: Zacharias Janssen and his father build one of the first compound microscopes: two lenses, one above the other, magnifying far more than one lens alone.
  • 1665: Robert Hooke looks at a thin slice of cork, sees rows of tiny empty boxes and calls them CELLS, after the small rooms in a monastery. He was looking at the cell walls of dead plant cells.
  • 1674: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, using a far better single-lens microscope he ground himself, sees living single-celled organisms in pond water and in scrapings from his own teeth. He called them animalcules: the first time anyone saw a living cell.
  • 1831: Robert Brown examines orchid leaves and identifies the NUCLEUS as a structure present in cells.
  • 1838: Matthias Schleiden, a botanist, concludes that all PLANTS are made of cells.
  • 1839: Theodor Schwann, a zoologist, concludes that all ANIMALS are made of cells too.
  • 1855: Rudolf Virchow states that every cell comes from a PRE-EXISTING cell (omnis cellula e cellula), contradicting spontaneous generation. Louis Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments a few years later provided the experimental evidence.
  • Notice the pattern: each step needed a better instrument first. Cell theory is a good example of technology driving science.

Cell theory

10 min · Activity 2

In your book, then here

3(a). Outline the THREE components of cell theory. [3]
Support hintWhat are ALL organisms made of? What is the smallest unit of life? Where does every cell come from (Virchow)?
3(b). Explain why Virchow's component was so important. What older idea did it replace? [2]
Support hintName the old idea. Say what Virchow showed instead about where cells come from (and who later proved it).
Challenge, for the class discussion. Cell theory says every organism is made of one or more cells. Yet a striated muscle fibre is one "cell" with many nuclei, and some fungi have long threads with no walls dividing them into separate cells at all. Does an exception destroy a theory, or refine it?

STEP 4 · TEST

Drawing a plant cell and an animal cell

15 min · Activity 3
  • These are generalised cells: diagrams showing the structures a typical cell has. No single real cell looks exactly like this.
  • Both cells have a nucleus, a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and mitochondria. Only the plant cell has a cell wall, chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole.
  • Rules for a scientific drawing: sharp pencil, single clean lines, no shading or colouring; large (at least half the page width); labels written horizontally with straight ruled lines that touch the structure and never cross.
  • Draw the two cells side by side in your book so you can compare them.

In your book, then here

4(a)(b). In your book, draw and label both cells (animal: nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, mitochondria; plant: all of those plus chloroplasts, permanent vacuole, cell wall). Then show here where each structure is found. [5]

STEP 5 · CHALLENGE

The light microscope: practical

30 min · Activity 4 · Worksheets 1 and 2

Worksheet 1 · The parts of the microscope and how to use it

  • Carry it with two hands: one on the arm, one under the base.
  • Place the slide on the stage, specimen over the hole, held by the stage clips.
  • Start with the LOWEST power objective (×4) and turn on the lamp.
  • Watching FROM THE SIDE, use the coarse focus to bring the objective close to the slide.
  • Look through the eyepiece and turn the coarse focus the OTHER way, raising the tube until the specimen appears. Never focus downwards while looking down the eyepiece.
  • Sharpen with the fine focus. Centre what you want before changing lenses.
  • Turn the nosepiece to a higher power, then use the FINE focus only.
  • When you finish: lowest power back in place, lamp off, slide removed and cleaned.
Total magnification. total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification. A ×10 eyepiece with the ×40 objective gives 10 × 40 = ×400. Write the TOTAL beside your drawing, not the objective.

Worksheet 2 · Observing plant and animal cells

▶ Preparing an onion and a cheek cell slideWatch before you start. Note how the coverslip is lowered at an angle to avoid air bubbles.
Method
Plant cells: onion epidermisPeel a thin, transparent layer from the inside of an onion scale with forceps. Lay it FLAT on a slide (a folded piece will never focus). Add one drop of iodine solution, then lower a coverslip slowly at an angle. Iodine stains the nucleus and cytoplasm.
Animal cells: cheek epitheliumOnly if your school permits it, with a clean cotton swab disposed of as your teacher directs. Rub the inside of your own cheek gently, smear the swab on a slide, add one drop of methylene blue, lower a coverslip at an angle. Never use anyone else's swab or slide.
SafetyIodine and methylene blue stain skin and clothes: wear goggles, wipe spills at once. Tell your teacher if a slide or coverslip breaks and do not pick up the pieces. Used swabs and slides go where your teacher tells you.
If you cannot prepare a slideUse the prepared slides provided. The recording and drawing are the same either way.
What to expect. Onion cells are rectangular, packed like bricks, each with a wall and one nucleus, and no chloroplasts (this layer never sees light). Cheek cells are irregular, flat and round-edged, spaced apart, with a nucleus and no wall. Air bubbles are perfect black-rimmed circles: they are not cells!

In your book, then here

6(a). For the slide you recorded: name the specimen and stain, and give eyepiece × objective and the total magnification. [2]
Support hintName BOTH the specimen and its stain. Multiply eyepiece × objective, e.g. 10 × 40 = ×400 (not just "×40").
6(b). In your book, make a scientific drawing of two or three cells (not the whole field of view) with at least three ruled labels. Here, list how many cells you drew and the labels you used. [3]
Support hintDraw only two or three cells. Label the nucleus. Onion: cell wall; cheek: cell membrane. Cytoplasm too.
6(c). State two differences you could actually SEE between the onion cells and the cheek cells. [2]
Support hintCompare shape, how they are arranged, and the outer boundary.
